chapter: Army band, Lena Horne, Billie Holiday and the 1950s
title: Drinking and discipline in his bands; firing trumpeter Hubert Dodson
summary: Horace rarely had drinking trouble in an organized band with steady personnel; he fired trumpeter Hubert Dodson for refusing to play a break and replaced him with Gail Brockman.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: This sort of brings up a topic. As a band leader through the years, how did you make out with regard to guys drinking on the job, and so on? Was that a major problem in just being responsible, getting to jobs on time and being there with the right clothes on, same colored socks, and so on?

I was fortunate in our band. I never had that trouble. I just had a couple of guys that I remember that would drink like that, but there were so many musicians in that time that you could get to replace these guys if they acted up, And jobs in big bands at that time -- Good jobs, I'm talking about were hard to come by, and especially steady jobs, where a year or a year and a half -- you know, the way you stay on the -- those are careers now.

So there were a lot of guys in Chicago just waiting for guys to goof, you know, and I only had one. There was a little guy named Hubert Dodson. He didn't become famous, but he was in that era along with Gene Ammonds, he came along with -- but he was an excellent reader, and he could play first, second, or third trumpet. He played beautifully, but he was weird, man, upstairs, you know. I remember one time, he was playing a solo, and he idolized Roy Eldridge, and he could play and he had good chops. And I remember one time, we were playing "After You're Gone," and we were playing it like Roy did with Krupa, you know, and when you got to the break in the bridge, he snatched his horn down, and instead of playing the break, he jumped to the mike. He says, "I'm not gonna play another note." And the guys, you know, thought it was funny. And he stood at attention. He was weird. I don't know. So he kept saying, "I'm not gonna play another note." So he kept saying it, so I begin to get a little peeved about it. I said, "Well, that's right, you're not. You're not gonna play another note. You're through." So I didn't even give him a notice, or one of those things. And this is when I got Gail Brockman, the guy that recorded with Gene Ammonds. Remember me telling you of "Redtop," and Gail took his place, and of course it was quite an addition to the group, because he was an excellent reader too. He could play. He had a beautiful style. But I never had any trouble with guys not

showing up on the job, getting drunk, or one of those things like -- I don't know. The guys wanted to play, I think, in those days, you know. They took it serious. It was a little bit different in my brother's band in that way, of course. But the guys knew how to hold their drinks. I shouldn't even say that. They knew how to hold the drinks. But playing in places like the Roseland on Broadway, you don't goof up jobs like that. So, I don't know if that answers your question or not, but the drinking thing didn't get out of hand. Didn't get out of hand. It was pretty well music.
Would you say that was pretty true with most all groups?

No. Number one, I had in those days what we would call an organized band, because we stayed together, the same personnel, for over a year. Then you gotta be classified as organized, you know, and with two or three sets of uniforms. But the guys in some groups figured that you had to drink that stuff to make you think you were playing up a storm, you know, and one of those things. I disagree with that. A lot of times, you might think you're doing it, so there's no way. But I have seen some musicians, though, that they really drank and could play. It's very seldom though that the two go together.
